teaching.causalExplanation: Start with what's in each bottle. A dissolved ionic compound isn't whole units floating around. It's separate ions, each surrounded by water. Silver nitrate solution is silver ions and nitrate ions. Sodium chloride solution is sodium ions and chloride ions. Mix them, and you have four kinds of ions in one tube. With salts like these, the only new thing that can happen is that ions find new partners. Silver ions and chloride ions attract each other more strongly than the water can keep them apart, so they lock together into solid silver chloride. A solid that forms when two solutions are mixed is a precipitate, and this is a precipitation reaction. Sodium and nitrate ions stay dissolved, exactly as they were. They take no part, so they're called spectator ions. They're in the tube, but they're not in the reaction. Which pairs lock together was found by experiment, and you can see the pattern on a small scale. Put one drop of each of two solutions into a well of a spotting plate, and record which pairs go cloudy. Wear safety glasses, use tiny volumes, and put the waste in the container your teacher labels. Silver nitrate stains skin, and lead and barium salts are toxic, so those are teacher demonstrations. Now look down the results. None of the solids contain sodium or nitrate.

scenes.teachingReason: Patterns like that are summed up as the solubility rules. A handy way to remember the soluble groups is NAGSAG. Nitrates, ammonium and Group 1 compounds are almost always soluble. Sulfates are soluble, except with barium, lead and calcium. Acetates are soluble. Everything else, like carbonates and hydroxides, is mostly insoluble, unless it's paired with Group 1 or ammonium.
